finalText:
**301 and 308 mean the same thing: the resource has a new permanent URL. The only real difference is the request method. After a 301, a client is allowed to turn a POST into a GET, and browsers do. After a 308, the client is expected to resend the same method and body.** Both are cacheable by default, and both are now defined in RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics, June 2022): 301 in §15.4.2 and 308 in §15.4.9.

**What each means**
- **301 Moved Permanently:** The resource "has been assigned a new permanent URI", and future requests should use the new one. The server SHOULD send a Location header with the preferred new URI, and the client MAY follow it automatically (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).
- **308 Permanent Redirect:** RFC 9110 uses almost the same words for 308. It also says the resource has a new permanent URI, the server SHOULD send Location, and the client MAY follow it automatically (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).

**Method and body**
- **General rule:** When a client follows a redirect automatically, RFC 9110 says it SHOULD resend the original request to the new URI. It changes the method only if that status code allows it. If the method becomes GET or HEAD, it removes the headers that describe the body, such as Content-Type and Content-Length (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).
- **301:** For historical reasons, the client "MAY change the request method from POST to GET". RFC 9110 suggests using 308 if you don't want that (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). Browsers do make this change. MDN says the Fetch Standard has browsers use GET after a 301 response to a POST (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/301).
  - **Why:** HTTP/1.0 originally meant 301 and 302 to keep the method. Browsers handled POST inconsistently, and most ended up switching to GET. So 307 and 308 were added as redirects that clearly keep the method, and the rules for 301 and 302 were relaxed to allow POST to become GET (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).
- **308:** The method must not change, so the body is sent again too. RFC 7538, which first defined 308, says it is like 301 "except that it does not allow changing the request method from POST to GET" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html). MDN says the method and body "will not be modified" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/308).
  - One detail: RFC 9110's own 308 section doesn't repeat this rule as a MUST NOT. (Its 307 section does.) The rule comes from the 3xx overview, which calls 307 and 308 the method-preserving redirects, plus the general instruction to resend the original request.

**Where the sources disagree.** MDN's 308 page says a 301 "requires the request method and the body to remain unchanged" and that older clients get this wrong (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/308). That doesn't match RFC 9110, which explicitly allows POST to become GET after a 301. It also doesn't match MDN's own 301 page, which calls that change "permitted by the HTTP specification". MDN's redirections guide takes a middle position: the original spec "did not intend to allow method changes", and some clients change the method anyway (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Redirections). RFC 9110 is the current standard, so a 301 is officially allowed to turn a POST into a GET.

**Caching.** RFC 9110 says both 301 and 308 are "heuristically cacheable". That means a cache may store them by default unless the method definition or Cache-Control headers say otherwise (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). RFC 7538 described 308 as "cacheable by default", which means the same thing in different words (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).

**History.** 301 has been in HTTP since HTTP/1.0. 308 was first published in Experimental RFC 7238, and then RFC 7538 (April 2015) made it a standard without technical changes. That filled the empty "permanent, keeps the method" slot next to 307 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html). RFC 9110 replaced RFC 7538 and RFC 7231, which had defined 301 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). RFC 7538 also warned that clients that don't recognise 308 treat it like 300 (Multiple Choices), so servers couldn't count on automatic redirection at first.
